limitations: Single tiny provisioned one-shard stream, one partition key, sequential signed HTTP calls, one bounded run; not a stress test or throughput benchmark.
Observed monotonic client elapsed time includes serialization/signing/network/service/decoding; it is not an AWS deterministic admission clock or timing guarantee.
No capacity increase, paid commitment, warm throughput, KMS key, consumer, trail or account-level setting was created or modified.
All attempted records and batches are below the configured 10-MiB decoded-data-plus-partition-key maximum; this experiment tests admission under bounded burst sequences, not oversize validation.

No automatic data retries: explicit post-idle writes use new identifiable records. Request cadence cannot isolate the hidden native refill algorithm or establish sustained PutRecord 10-MiB/s throughput.
No write throttle observed within the predetermined bound; the write quota boundary was not reached. No larger/faster follow-up load was attempted.
No read-rate or cooldown exception observed in this run; network latency and returned page sizes prevent treating this as a disproof of documented limits.

Large-request client durations ranged from 6.535412 to 13.374903 seconds; sequential upload/response cadence left native refill opportunities. No partial-batch throttle can be concluded from all-success batches.

findings.finding: ACTIVE single-shard PROVISIONED stream reports MaxRecordSizeInKiB 10240 before data calls. All 49 attempted records were accepted; three 9-MiB PutRecord requests and mixed PutRecords requests returned HTTP 200.

All seven PutRecords batches returned FailedRecordCount 0, with success entries correlating by index. Mixed large/tiny batches and four 256-KiB-record/tiny sibling batches did not induce quota saturation; no partial-success error entries were observed or synthesized.

Following a measured 12.000079-second no-call idle, a new 9-MiB-plus-64-byte mixed batch and a new 64-byte PutRecord succeeded. This is post-idle admission evidence, not demonstrated recovery from an observed throttle.

Eight GetRecords calls read all 49 accepted sequence numbers with exact decoded-byte equality, including 64-byte tiny, 256-KiB, 3-MiB and 9-MiB records. No read throttle or cooldown error was observed.

One native GetRecords response contained 10485824 decoded Data bytes (10 MiB + 64 bytes). The next sequential call returned 128 bytes successfully. These are observed native page boundaries, not a guaranteed 10-MiB ceiling or cooldown exemption.

No write quota boundary was reached in 65012778 attempted decoded data-plus-key bytes and 105.902689 active seconds. Client transfer latency and native burst capacity are not isolated by this experiment; no deterministic timer, steady-rate or token-bucket size is inferred.
